svg.title: Mathematics prerequisite graph
svg.desc: 48 concepts and 80 directed prerequisite relationships, progressing from arithmetic foundations to introductory algebra.

g.text: 48 concepts · 80 relationships · Grades 5–9 and earlier foundations
Read top to bottom: prerequisite → dependent concept. Every arrow is PREREQUISITE_OF. Grade bands are approximate.

a.xlink:title: Place-value units explain regrouping in addition and subtraction.
Number-line magnitude and order extend to positions below zero.
Variables stand for numbers or numerical quantities.
Combining equal groups and repeated subtraction ground multiplication and division.
Integer addition and subtraction extend whole-number combining and difference operations.
Factors and multiples describe exact multiplication and division relationships.
Equal sharing and division ground the interpretation of fractions as quotients.
Integer products and quotients extend whole-number multiplication and division.
Ratios express multiplicative comparisons rather than additive differences.
Positive whole-number powers abbreviate repeated multiplication.
Arithmetic operations provide meaning for reordering and regrouping sums and products.
Equal-group multiplication explains distributing a factor across a sum.
Arithmetic operations give meaning to performing the same operation on both sides.
Familiar arithmetic operations provide the pairs whose actions can be undone.
Common factors explain simplifying fractions without changing their value.
Fraction units explain why different numerator–denominator pairs can represent one quantity.
Fraction quantities ground fractional scaling and division by fractional amounts.
Decimal places represent fractional units with powers-of-ten denominators.
Equivalent fractions provide common units for addition and subtraction.
Equivalent fractions connect terminating decimals to simplified fractional representations.
Equivalent fractions support recognizing and scaling equivalent ratios.
Equivalent fractional units support locating rational coordinates on differently scaled axes.
Signed fractional sums retain the need for common fractional units.
Signed fractional products and quotients extend fraction multiplication and division.
Rates involving fractional quantities require division of fractions.
Reciprocals explain negative exponents and quotients of powers.
Decimal computation depends on tracking the value of each place.
Decimal division produces decimal representations of fractions.
Mixed fraction–decimal calculations require compatible numerical representations.
Fraction–decimal equivalence connects the numerical representations of percentages.
Signed positions and opposites explain integer sums and differences.
Signed number-line positions determine coordinates in all four quadrants.
Signed addition patterns and additive inverses help explain multiplication sign rules.
Combining integer exponents requires signed addition and subtraction.
Integer sign rules extend to multiplication and division of rational numbers.
Evaluation at signed rational inputs requires rational-number arithmetic.
Rewriting expressions with rational coefficients requires signed rational arithmetic.
A unit rate expresses a ratio with one unit of the reference quantity.
Percent expresses a multiplicative comparison per hundred.
A common unit rate identifies and generates proportional pairs.
Proportional scaling connects a percentage, its reference whole, and its corresponding amount.
Proportional reasoning establishes the constant multiplier represented across tables, equations, and graphs.
Percent calculations require interpreting the percentage as a numerical rate.
Repeated multiplication explains the initial exponent laws.
Evaluating expressions containing powers requires understanding exponent notation.
Operation precedence determines an expression’s grouping and structure.
Reordering and regrouping allow like terms to be collected.
Distribution and its reverse justify expansion, factoring, and combining like terms.
An equation asserts equality, which its solutions must make true.
Equality-preserving transformations depend on understanding equality as a relation.
Reading algebraic expressions requires interpreting their variable symbols.
Variables identify the quantities whose corresponding values are tracked.
Substitution requires identifying variable occurrences and preserving expression structure.
Identifying terms and coefficients makes valid expression rewriting possible.
Substitution and evaluation establish whether a proposed value satisfies an equation.
Testing candidate values requires evaluating the expressions being compared.
Evaluating y = kx connects its equation to table entries and plotted points.
Evaluating a function rule requires substituting inputs into an expression.
General linear equations require expanding expressions and collecting like terms.
Solving requires understanding what counts as a solution.
A simultaneous solution must satisfy each individual equation.
Valid transformations preserve the equation’s solution set.
Inverse operations undo operations surrounding the unknown.
Linear equation solving supplies variable-isolation procedures that inequalities adapt.
Rearranging linear equations and solving for intercepts support graphing different equation forms.
Substitution and elimination reduce systems to linear equations in one variable.
Solving an inequality requires understanding its ordered comparison and solution set.
Coordinate plotting turns proportional value pairs into a graph.
Tables of corresponding values represent how proportional quantities vary together.
Input–output correspondence makes the unique-output condition meaningful.
Two-variable system solutions specify corresponding values as ordered pairs.
Proportional representations provide the constant-rate case extended by adding an initial value.
Constant rate of change gives conceptual meaning to the slope calculation.
Slope determines a line’s direction and the changes between its points.
Connections among line equations, slopes, and intercepts support constructing linear models.
Graphical system solving requires constructing and interpreting both lines.
Function notation names the output assigned to a specified input.
A linear function model assigns one predicted output to each allowed input.
Algebraic system solving seeks values that satisfy every equation together.
Shared graph points represent simultaneous satisfaction of the equations.
Interpret whole numbers using base-ten units, relative size, and positions on a number line.
Combine, separate, and compare whole-number quantities, including regrouping across place values.
Reason about equal groups, multiplicative comparisons, products, and quotients.
Identify divisibility relationships, including common factors and common multiples.
Interpret a fraction as a number, a quantity of equal-sized parts, and a quotient.
Generate, recognize, and simplify fractions that represent the same number.
Add and subtract nonnegative fractions by expressing quantities in common fractional units.
Multiply and divide nonnegative fractions using scaling, grouping, and reciprocal relationships.
Interpret decimal digits as tenths, hundredths, and successive powers-of-ten fractional units.
Add, subtract, multiply, and divide nonnegative decimals while accounting for place value.
Express fractions as terminating or repeating decimals and terminating decimals as fractions.
Interpret positive and negative integers, opposites, zero, and order on a number line.
Add and subtract integers using signed changes, opposites, and additive inverses.
Multiply and divide integers with consistent reasoning about signs.
Compute with positive and negative fractions and decimals, including mixed representations.
Interpret an ordered comparison of quantities in multiplicative terms.
Determine and interpret an amount per one unit, including rates involving fractions.
Recognize equivalent ratios and determine missing quantities through consistent multiplicative scaling.
Interpret percent as a rate per hundred and express it using fractions and decimals.
Determine a part, whole, percentage, or percent change using proportional relationships.
Interpret and evaluate powers with positive whole-number exponents as repeated multiplication.
Apply product, quotient, and power laws, including zero and negative exponents with appropriate nonzero bases.
Evaluate numerical expressions using grouping, exponents, and conventional operation precedence.
Recognize when reordering or regrouping addition or multiplication preserves a value.
Understand why multiplying a sum or difference equals combining the corresponding products.
Interpret the equals sign as asserting that two quantities or expressions have the same value.
Interpret a symbol as an unknown, a varying quantity, or an arbitrary number.
Read and construct expressions, identifying terms, coefficients, factors, powers, and grouping.
Replace variables with specified rational values and compute the resulting expression.
Rewrite linear expressions with rational coefficients through distribution, factoring, and combining like terms.
Interpret an equation as a condition and a solution as a value that makes it true.
Preserve equality by applying the same valid operation to both sides, avoiding division by zero.
Recognize how addition and subtraction, and multiplication and division, undo one another.
Solve rational-coefficient linear equations, including variables on both sides and zero, one, or infinitely many solutions.
Interpret inequalities as ordered comparisons and describe satisfying values, including number-line representations.
Isolate a variable while preserving the solution set, reversing order when multiplying or dividing by a negative.
Locate and interpret ordered pairs on scaled perpendicular axes, including negative and fractional coordinates.
Represent corresponding values of two varying quantities using ordered pairs and tables.
Connect equivalent-ratio tables, equations of the form y = kx, and straight-line graphs through the origin.
Recognize a constant rate of change between quantities, allowing a nonzero initial value.
Interpret and calculate Δy/Δx as a line’s rate of change; recognize undefined slope for vertical lines.
Graph two-variable linear equations using slope, intercepts, or equivalent forms, including horizontal and vertical lines.
Recognize a correspondence that assigns exactly one output to each allowed input.
Interpret f(x) as an output and evaluate a function rule at specified inputs.
Construct a linear function from a table, graph, two points, or contextual rate and initial value.
Interpret a linear system’s solution as an ordered pair satisfying every equation simultaneously.
Solve two-variable linear systems through substitution or elimination and identify the number of solutions.
Determine or estimate shared solutions from intersecting, parallel, or coincident lines.
